Reconstruction record

The book follows the argument to the critical line. As of 21 November 2026, we estimate that about 85% of the explanatory work is written (roughly 79–91%). The estimate weights six parts by the writing each requires. The real period chapter now follows a derivative through the finite layers and proves invariance under translation. The Galois chapter now derives the tangent matrix from the local jumps and constructs the extracted representation using the scalar diagonal blocks and the action of each component. The Hecke chapter now derives the one-place dimension bound and the ℓ-adic correction on a finite group. It also explains how the weight gaps are chosen and why the conjugate eigenforms fit in one finite-dimensional space. A separate period calculation recovers the jumps of the limit from its moments.

  • On restriction to the smaller unitary group a bound on one trial vector becomes an inequality on an entire invariant space. A three-coordinate example illustrates which directions and which test vector survive. The negative derivative can land in an earlier layer, and a uniform Taylor step passes from those layers to the group. A separate formal-degree calculation tests whether one copy fills a space of coefficients. The invariant space · A threshold coordinate · The isometric copy.
  • A specified set of good split primes realizes every finite Galois test after finitely many exclusions. The trace-limit argument constructs an odd-rank representation, and the two lifts give the same remaining polynomial after character subtraction. The construction from a cohomological eigenspace uses a rank-extraction theorem. The simultaneous congruence argument uses density of automorphic forms, integral coordinates, auxiliary types and change of weight. Two primes for one test · Recovering a representation from its traces · Removing one line.
  • The norm of the final minor includes the different of the real field. The joint estimate for two lists counts their shared row once. The two-field calculation shows where the discriminant enters the dimension argument.
  • At fixed determinant, the number of possible sets of bad places and the allowed mass per set have reciprocal factors. The mass on the perpendicular line enters separately. Two hyperplanes at the same order · The line cutoff · Summing the masses.
  • A regular unit shift supplies a model of the discrete series. Averaging matrix coefficients and contracting a double tensor explain why each such model occurs exactly once. A shift at a wall · The averaging maps · Multiplicity one.
  • For fixed discriminant order, an ideal records which rational subspaces can lie in the same orbit. Two projections then identify the common residue classes that govern the integral intersections. Counting the ideals · One orbit, different intersections · The discriminant bound.
  • The real period needs an ordered differential minor and an estimate for a translated vector. One calculation recovers a projector from a simple polynomial root. A different estimate controls the cost of taking two real derivatives after translation. Isolating the projector · Bounding the translated derivative.
  • The smaller unitary quotient has finite volume. In an isotropic shell this contributes a constant factor, while the scalar variable contributes an exponential in height. The quotient and a circle example · The volume identity.
  • For the global dimension estimate, marking a maximal lattice bounds the mass at a given discriminant. Separately, arithmetic congruences control matrices whose singular values are close to one. The two mass bounds · The distance to the identity.
  • The real period uses two estimates for different purposes. The lowest compact type gives decay away from the compact subgroup. A second representation on the stabilizer gives a vector with positive period. The product of minors · The positive eigenvalue.
  • A term in the bottom period is an integral over the stabilizer of a vector. Its decay depends on how far the translating isometry moves that vector. The comparison with the identity term carries the same Haar factors through the local and adelic integrals. The coefficient estimate · One class in the period.
  • In an isotropic shell the remaining rational variable is a single scalar. Finite-place conditions put it in a lattice. At the real places a volume comparison bounds the number of its points in a growing box. The first nonzero points.
  • The cohomological bound uses an exact integral complex of arithmetic faces. Cutting a convex set explains how to fill a cycle whose vertices have no common witness. A determinant calculation then bounds the number of faces up to symmetry, and the order of a stabilizer controls its positive-degree homology. Filling the cycle · Bounding the coordinates · The stabilizer calculation.

The analytic chapters follow a possible zero from its residue to the one-sided window estimate and reflection. The theta chapters reconstruct an integral expansion at the selected primes, the local zeta quotients, the two Siegel–Weil ranges and the absolute bound for pairing two lifts. The arithmetic chapter derives the marked-window selection, degree-two estimate and separate character counts. Each chapter records its remaining inputs. The chapter on normalization follows the six prime classes and the nonzero base tuple. The arithmetic chapter constructs the finite cycles and their determinant evaluations. The book follows the length of an inert lattice into the local zeta sum. At a real place the projection of a joint polynomial gives the positive factor. The Fourier comparison recovers the lower-range value after treating singular frequencies. The count of rational classes at fixed height supplies the convergence estimate. Counting integral Hermitian frames gives the full-rank Whittaker factor at the good finite places. At an exceptional place shell cancellation supplies the continued value. At infinity determinant differentiation continues the nonsingular coefficient and recovers its density. The global Gram-fibre mean explains how the local densities fit together. In cohomology, transference bounds the distance to the lattice, and products of translation classes determine the weights in the stabilizer. The common invariant functions explain why a spectral gap bounds the period of a mean-zero form. A change of volume on Hermitian matrices explains how to bound the integral on the compact set. Averaging the vertices transfers that bound to the period of a fixed cycle. A second Hecke estimate forces the remaining periods to vanish, and alternating traces bound the number of independent tests. The split-sequence calculation supplies integral stability, while the cyclotomic quotient map bounds the length at the base field. In the dyadic tower the indices of Frobenius subgroups bound the number of inertia evaluations. The choice of primes uses a count of characters with a zero and a mean square for quadratic twists. Further inputs include local representation densities and the volume estimates for the period maps. An end-to-end review of the exposition is still in progress. Current project state

  10. Ordered products of edge characters are invariant real cocycles

    For a free abelian group A of finite rank, the homogeneous j-cochain Cα evaluates j real additive characters on successive edge increments and multiplies the resulting scalars, with no factorial. It is invariant and closed.

    Hypotheses. Trivial real coefficients. The affine application uses positive degree j=q+1. Each j-cochain takes j+1 vertices; simultaneous translation of all vertices preserves its value.

    Formulas. additive cup word

  13. A common finite denominator and an archimedean lattice

    A compact family of vectors in (𝔸_F⊗_F E)^M lies in a coordinate box with one positive integer denominator N at all finite places and one archimedean ℓ¹ radius r>0. Within that denominator, the rational coordinate subgroup is (N⁻¹𝒪_F)^(2M), embedded in real dimension 2[F:ℚ]M.

    Hypotheses. F is totally real and E/F is CM quadratic. Fix an F-basis of E. The local integral lattices are taken in the chosen coefficient basis of the two-dimensional algebra over F_v. They are compact open, including at split places.

  15. A uniform cutoff and growth bound for the dilated rational count

    For compact Ω and the scalar flow, the count of nonzero X∈E^M with τ(−x)X∈Ω vanishes for x<x₀ and is at most C exp(2[F:ℚ]M x) for x≥x₀. For Ω⊂B_N(r) one can choose x₀=log(r₀/r), C=(5r/r₀)^ν whenever the positive radius r₀≤1 gives P_N(r₀)=1.

    Hypotheses. The scalar flow acts by exp(x) at the real places and by one at finite places. The radius r₀ is strictly below all positive real sizes in B_N(1), unless that set of nonzero vectors is empty. In the isotropic shell application the compact set is an image under the Hermitian pairing and M=1 in this counting theorem.

  188. Summing the carries and recovering the primitive valuation

    For an odd prime ℓ and level F=f_{ℓ′}ℓ^m, k=e+1≥2 and a primitive character of the selected parity, let χ be its induced character at F.   216. Self-dual normalization preserves the product of local Gram densities

    For self-dual source and target Haar measures, the continuous density at an invertible target is the integral over its reference Gram fibre multiplied by cᵥ/eᵥ. These ratios have product one including infinity. Hence the archimedean density times the convergent product of finite densities equals the normalized rational Gram mean.

  295. Why the good model needs a congruence at an auxiliary principal prime

    A prescribed inertia element at the target agrees on the roots of an integral monic polynomial for J and in the Artin class quotient with an arithmetic Frobenius φ at a degree-one auxiliary prime ideal 𝔮. The trivial Artin class of inertia makes 𝔮 principal. At 𝔮, φ(J)≡J^q≡J. Avoiding the finite exceptional set where roots collide then forces equality in characteristic zero and hence inertia fixes J.

  296. The repeated Fourier factors produce a square at a CM point

    For any principal prime ideal 𝔮 of the quadratic field with prime norm q, the CM endomorphism of determinant q fixes the period point. A factor of G_q vanishes. At that point (J^q−J)^2=(1−ζ_q)r with r integral, and (J^q−J)^(2q)=q r₀ r^q with r₀ integral. Thus J^q−J reduces to zero at every place over 𝔮.

  300. The exact excess length and the two thresholds

  329. The inverse-character partner of a Jacobi sum

  461. Positive prime moments bound a list of shifted zero distances containing the target

    A prime failure injects into a bad primitive character since fp=f′p′ and f′≤F<p forces p=p′. The ratio of the zero-density exception count to the population is O(U^(−21/40)).   604. A finite stabilizer kills its positive-degree integral homology by its order

    For a transitive nonempty G-set X with stabilizer S, H_j(G,ℤ[X])≅H_j(S,ℤ) in all degrees. If S has finite order h, the norm and augmentation through ℤ[S] show that multiplication by h vanishes on H_j(S,ℤ) for j>0. Their degree-zero composite multiplies ℤ by h.

    Hypotheses. G is a discrete group, X a left G-set and x a specified point. Coefficients on the stabilizer are integral and trivial in the application. Finiteness is required only for the norm of all elements and the order bound.

  613. Carries annihilate ideal classes in a cyclotomic field

  666. Finite Fourier interpolation computes the good Whittaker integral
